title: Making It Safe to Speak in the NICU
text:
Hospitals are steep hierarchies. Doctors sit near the top, while nurses, respiratory therapists and other staff sit lower, and lower status people often hesitate to raise concerns. In 2006 Ingrid Nembhard and Amy Edmondson studied how leaders could change that.

They surveyed more than a thousand staff members in 23 neonatal intensive care units in the United States and Canada. All of the units were taking part in a shared program to improve care for premature babies. The researchers measured how psychologically safe staff felt, meaning whether they believed they could speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes without being punished or humiliated. They also measured what they called leader inclusiveness: the extent to which the leading physicians invited others' views and showed they valued them.

As expected, professional status mattered. Physicians felt safer than nurses, and nurses safer than other staff. But in units where physician leaders were inclusive, the gap shrank, and lower status staff felt much safer. Greater psychological safety, in turn, was linked to stronger engagement in the units' improvement work.
lesson: People lower in the hierarchy speak up only when those at the top clearly invite them. Ask for input in words and show you value it in deeds.
location: Neonatal intensive care units in the USA and Canada
source: Nembhard, I. M., and Edmondson, A. C. (2006). Making it safe: The effects of leader inclusiveness and professional status on psychological safety and improvement efforts in health care teams. Journal of Organizational Behavior, 27(7), 941-966.
